questions.q: What is the programme mainly about?
options: How bitter foods may be good for our health
The dangers of eating far too much sugar every day
questions.why: Phil says they'll be finding out how bitter foods can benefit our health.

questions.q: How does Phil feel about grapefruit?
options: He's allergic to it, so he has never been able to eat it
He doesn't like it much because it's too bitter
questions.why: He says he's not that keen on grapefruit because they're too bitter for him.

questions.q: Why does Beth say “maybe you should take my grapefruit”?
options: Because she doesn't want to eat it herself
Because bitter food could be good for him
questions.why: She has just said bitter food has been linked to a number of health benefits.

questions.q: According to Leyla Kazim, what can bitter foods do?
questions.why: She says they can suppress feelings of hunger, as well as control glucose release.

questions.q: What role does the gut microbiome play, according to Beth?
questions.why: She says microorganisms in our gut play an important role in the digestive process.

questions.q: What does chef Alexina Anatole say about bitter food?
options: Most people eat very little of it
It should only ever be eaten in very small amounts
People eat much more of it than they realise
It is too expensive for most people
questions.why: She says people are exposed to bitters way more than they think they are.

questions.q: Why does Alexina think people dislike the idea of bitterness?
options: Because it is linked with negative feelings as well as food
Because bitter food is hard to find
Because children are always taught by their parents to avoid it
questions.why: She says there's a perception of bitter and negativity, in emotions and in food.

questions.q: Which common bitter things does Alexina mention?
questions.why: When asked for examples, she says, “Chocolate, coffee, alcohol.”
